payload.title: Fix TypeError crash in task show --text when field content is bytes
payload.description: endless task show <id> --text crashes with 'TypeError: write() argument must be str, not bytes' for at least one task. Traceback: task_cmd.py _render_detail_human -> _echo_large_section -> _echo_field_body -> click.echo(content) -> the wrapper write() in task_cmd.py, which forwards to self._dest.write(s) where s is bytes. The stdout wrapper class assumes str. Reproduce with a task whose stored text triggers it; find why the field arrives as bytes (encoding on the way in, or the pager/color wrapper path) and fix at the source rather than coercing at the write boundary. Any task whose text is unreadable is effectively lost to the CLI, so this is a data-access bug, not cosmetic.

fields.text:
# E-1889 — Make reopening your own landed work the documented, tooled norm

Absorbs E-1890 (tooling counterpart). Every decision below is settled; there are
no open questions. Where a choice had a plausible alternative, the rejected one
is recorded so it is not relitigated.

## Problem

Agents reflexively file a new task for a bug they just introduced rather than
reopening the task that introduced it. The result is backlog growth.

A backlog is never free, on any project. Every filed task is a standing claim on
future attention: it must be read, re-read, and triaged past on every pass,
whether or not it is ever worked. A task filed reflexively does not defer the
cost of the discovery — it converts a small immediate cost into a recurring one.

On Endless itself that cost is currently visible as pending worktrees gating a
planned Python-to-Go port, but that is one instance of the cost, not the reason
for it.

Reproduced live in the E-1845 session: four tasks filed during one task, two of
which (E-1888, E-1891) turned out to be a single defect and had to be merged
afterward, and one of which (E-1894) rested on a category error and was retired.

The cause is not agent carelessness. The handoff template instructs exactly this
behavior.

## Settled decisions

| # | Decision | Rejected alternative |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `task reopen` is aligned to land `revisit`, like the other two reopen paths. Code change, not just docs. | Documenting the three paths' divergence as intentional. |
| 2 | Five templates get the full rewording; `brainstorm` keeps "file as new tasks" (that IS its deliverable) and gains only the root-cause test. | One wording across all six. |
| 3 | Mermaid gains `confirmed`/`assumed`/`completed` → `revisit`. `declined`/`obsolete` stay terminal in the diagram. | Drawing all five reopenable statuses. |
| 4 | Tooling folds into E-1889; E-1890 is absorbed and marked obsolete. | Keeping E-1890 for the recently-landed hint. |
| 5 | Claim promotion gains `revisit`. | Routing `spawn --reopen` through re-approval. |
| 6 | `_REOPEN_TO_REVISIT` narrows to E-1555's set; `declined`/`obsolete` are no longer implicitly revived. | Broadening `task reopen` to accept them. |
| 7 | Handoff uses the four-case bulleted form. | Compact prose; minimal edit. |
| 8 | `revisit` definition broadens to a two-case sentence. | Terse form; form with explicit pointer. |
| 9 | Guide pattern lives in `orchestration.md`, cross-referenced from `tasks.md`. | `tasks.md` only; `orchestration.md` with no pointer. |
| 10 | Verification splits by durability: behavior into the real suites, acceptance into the verify script. | Everything in one verify script. |
| 11 | `session resume --reopen` on `declined`/`obsolete` refuses loudly and names the explicit route. | Silently skipping the flip; a `--force` override. |

## A. Handoff templates

Under `internal` templatecmd templates handoff. Five files carry byte-identical
text at the noted lines: `todo.md.tmpl:12`, `bugfix.md.tmpl:14`,
`epic.md.tmpl:25`, `research.md.tmpl:14`, `respawn.md.tmpl:45`. Replace with:

```
4. Stay focused on E-{{.spawned_id}}. For anything you discover along the way:
   - Could it reasonably be done now, inside the work already underway? Do it —
     note it in the commit message, and add a `discovery` note to
     `endless task report`.
   - Is it a bug in work THIS session landed? Reopen that task
     (`endless task update E-NNN --status revisit`) and fix it there.
   - Otherwise file it (`--cleans-up E-{{.spawned_id}}`) and confirm before
     implementing.
   - Filing more than one? Check whether they share a root cause — file the
     cause, not each symptom.
```

"Report it" is spelled out deliberately: the earlier draft said only "do it,
and report it", which is the kind of vagueness that makes a bullet ignorable.
The two halves do different jobs — the commit message records WHAT changed, the
`discovery` note records THAT the session went beyond its brief. Without the
note the user has to read the diff to learn scope grew. `task report --json`
already accepts `{"kind": "discovery"}` and bounces entries it judges
ceremonial, so that filter — not the agent's judgment of significance — is the
guard against noise.

`respawn.md.tmpl` uses hyphen bullets with no step number; adapt the list marker
to match its surrounding style, keeping the four cases verbatim.

`brainstorm.md.tmpl:16` keeps its existing sentence — for a brainstorm, emitting
tasks and decisions IS the deliverable — and gains one line:

```
   Filing more than one? Check whether they share a root cause — file the
   cause, not each symptom.
```

## B. Canonical status lifecycle

Edit `docs/status-lifecycle.mmd`, then re-sync the three byte-identical copies
in `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and `docs/guide/index.md`. Add:

```
    confirmed --> revisit: shipped work found wrong
    assumed --> revisit: shipped work found wrong
    completed --> revisit: shipped work found wrong
```

Keep the existing `confirmed --> [*]`, `assumed --> [*]`, `completed --> [*]`
edges — those statuses remain ordinary end states; the new edges say the door is
not locked.

`declined` and `obsolete` deliberately gain no edge (decision 6 removes the only
implicit path that revived them).

## C. `revisit` definition

`docs/guide/index.md`, the status table:

```
| `revisit` | Needs re-evaluation before it can proceed — either a partial plan
that no longer holds, or work that shipped and turned out wrong. Reopening your
own landed work lands here. |
```

The mermaid's existing `unplanned --> revisit: needs re-evaluation` label stays
as-is; the new edges carry the shipped-work case.

Note: the same table's `declined` row says "Requires `--reason`". Verified
correct — `--reason` is `task decline`'s flag, stored as outcome. Do not
"fix" it.

## D. Guide pattern — "Fix a bug in your own landed work"

New section in `docs/guide/orchestration.md`, near the existing `--reopen`
material (currently around the `task spawn --reopen` line). It must cover:

1. **The judgment.** A bug in work you just landed is not new work. Reopen the
   task that introduced it rather than filing a peer.
2. **The mechanics.** `task update <id> --status revisit`, then reuse the
   task's existing worktree rather than creating a second one for the same work.
3. **Re-verification.** The task's verify script still exists and still applies;
   re-run it rather than authoring a second one.
4. **The boundary.** When a genuinely separate task IS right — the discovery is
   new work the conversation surfaced, not a defect in what shipped.

One-line cross-reference from `tasks.md` under the status material, pointing
here.

## E. Code — reopen alignment

1. **`_reopen_task_core`** (`src/endless/task_cmd.py`, around the
   `new_status = "ready" if text_present else "unplanned"` line): always
   `revisit`. Keep returning `text_present` — callers use it for the message
   suffix — but stop branching status on it. Update the `reopen_item` docstring,
   which currently says "back to `ready` or `unplanned`".

2. **Five stale help/comment sites** assert the old target and must be updated
   in the same change: `task_cmd.py` at the spawn-reopen docstring, the
   `--reopen` help string, and the two reopen pre-step comments; plus the
   matching `--reopen` help text in `cli.py`.

3. **`_REOPEN_TO_REVISIT`** (`src/endless/session_cmd.py`): narrow to
   `{confirmed, assumed, completed}`, matching `_REOPENABLE_TERMINAL_STATUSES`.
   In `_resolve_resume`, refuse when `--reopen` targets a `declined`/`obsolete`
   task:

   ```
   Error: E-123 is 'declined' — a deliberate decision, not dormant work.
   Reviving it is an explicit act:
       endless task update E-123 --status revisit
   Then resume without --reopen.
   ```

   Follows the loud-failure-on-invalid-state convention used by the verb,
   maybe-parent, and db gates.

4. **Claim promotion** (`internal/monitor/session.go`): add `revisit` to the
   `status IN (...)` set. Without it, `task spawn --reopen` would bind a session
   and leave the task reading as not-started. The background-session gate is a
   separate check and is unchanged — background sessions remain restricted to
   `ready`.

## F. Code — three file-time hints

All three fire from `task add`. **Hints, never refusals** — sometimes a
genuinely separate task IS right, and the distinction needs human judgment.
Follow the existing gate/hint conventions.

1. **Recently landed.** When `--cleans-up X` names a task that the CURRENT
   session landed within 24h (join `task_landings` on `task_id` + `session_id`,
   filter `landed_at`), print: *"E-X was landed by this session Nh ago —
   consider `task update E-X --status revisit` and fixing it there."*

2. **Backlog pressure.** Print the count of open (`untriaged`/`unplanned`)
   tasks in the project, so the cost of adding one is visible at the moment the
   decision is made.

3. **Same-session root cause.** When this session has already filed at least one
   task (its `surfaced` rows in `session_tasks`), list them and ask whether the
   new one shares a root cause with any — *"file the cause, not the symptoms."*

   This is the mechanism that would have caught E-1888/E-1891. E-1739's
   semantic-dup gate provably would NOT have: those two were different files,
   different tuples, different symptoms, not semantically similar — yet one
   defect. Backlog-wide *similarity* and same-session *common cause* are
   different checks; E-1739 stays independent and is not superseded.

## Verification

**Real suites — permanent invariants:**

- pytest: `task reopen` lands `revisit` from each of the three reopenable
  statuses; `session resume --reopen` refuses on `declined`/`obsolete` and still
  works on the three; each hint fires when its condition holds and stays silent
  otherwise; no hint ever blocks the add.
- go test: claim promotion moves `revisit` → `underway`; the background-session
  gate still refuses non-`ready`.
- Mermaid byte-identity across the three copies belongs here too — it is a
  permanent invariant currently asserted in three separate verify scripts
  (e-1648, e-1832, e-1845). Promote it to a real test as part of this task and
  the copies stop multiplying.

**`tests/tasks/e-1889-verify.sh` — point-in-time acceptance only:**

- the four-case wording is present in all five templates;
- `brainstorm.md.tmpl` retains its own sentence and gained the root-cause line;
- the guide pattern section exists in `orchestration.md` with the cross-reference
  from `tasks.md`;
- the `revisit` table row reads as specified.

## Absorbed / superseded

- **E-1890** — absorbed. Mark obsolete with an outcome naming this task. Its
  recently-landed hint is section F.1 verbatim, including the 24h window and the
  hint-never-refusal constraint.
- **E-1739** — NOT superseded. Different check (see F.3).
- **E-1623** — unaffected, but note that promoting the mermaid assertion into a
  real test removes one of the duplicated blocks it would otherwise retrofit.



---

## Addendum — what actually landed, beyond the plan above

Recorded after the fact so the branch's contents are legible without reading
five commit messages. Everything here landed on E-1889's branch; nothing below
was in the plan when it was approved.

### 1. Rebase onto E-1822's handoff refactor

The plan says deliverable A edits five templates carrying byte-identical text.
Between approval and landing, E-1822 extracted that text into a shared
`handoff_focus` partial in `internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/_mechanics.tmpl`.
The four-case wording therefore landed in ONE place, not five, and reaches a
sixth consumer the plan never mentioned — `claim.md.tmpl`, the
claimed-into-a-live-session handoff. `respawn.md.tmpl` still carries its own
copy, because E-1822 deliberately left it out of the shared mechanics: a future
edit to this wording needs both files. The reopen command also picked up
`--db main`, matching E-1822's worktree-routing convention.

Equivalent rendered result, better factoring, but the plan's "five files"
framing no longer describes the tree.

### 2. Supervisor test timing (commit 049fcba5)

`go test ./...` failed during verification on a machine running several
parallel task sessions: `TestSupervisorSetsProcessGroup` exceeded a 2s
post-signal wait. All three supervisor tests in
`internal/sandboxcmd/sandbox_test.go` asserted timing on top of the behavior
under test. The two shutdown waits moved to a named `shutdownWait` of 10s
(matching `waitFor`'s existing deadline in the same file), and the two
grandchild-reaped checks — single-shot polls taken the instant `Run` returned,
racing an asynchronous signal/reparent/reap — now poll via a shared
`assertReaped`. Assertions unchanged; only the timing assumptions.

Unrelated to reopen semantics. Folded in because it blocked this task's own
verification, and it was one root cause across one file.

### 3. Verify-suite prohibition, violated and reverted (commit c7f3f234)

This branch violated the rule in `docs/guide/orchestration.md` that a per-task
verify suite is a land-time gate, not a standing regression suite:

- `tests/tasks/e-1845-verify.sh` was edited to relax an assertion this task's
  own change to `internal/monitor/session.go` had broken;
- `tests/tasks/e-1872-verify.sh` was edited to track this task's guide rewrite;
- `tests/tasks/e-1889-verify.sh` invoked `e-1872-verify.sh` as a regression
  gate, and four landed suites were run as evidence of correctness.

All reverted before landing. Both scripts are byte-identical to their
pre-E-1889 state and will now FAIL if run, which is correct — they assert
wording their own tasks landed against. `e-1889-verify.sh` section F ends after
`pytest tests/` and carries a comment stating why nothing else belongs there.

The durable fix is E-1916 (hook-level enforcement), whose plan was updated from
this session to cover both suite forms rather than only the `.sh` form.

### 4. Verify suite id casing (commit 1cc9dd43)

Out of scope for reopen semantics; landed here at the user's direction rather
than as a separate task.

`.endless/tasks/E-1758/` was the only Endless path writing a task id uppercase
— `.endless/worktrees/e-1889/` and `tests/tasks/e-1889-verify.sh` are
lowercase. The cause was `verify.Discover`'s exact `eff.Task != id` compare
against the manifest's canonical `task = "E-1758"` field: an internal equality
check was dictating an on-disk convention.

Fixed at the comparison rather than by picking a winner. `verify.NormalizeTaskID`
folds ids; discovery compares normalized and keys the returned map by the
manifest's own value, so a lookup of `E-1758` still hits (the Python CLI always
shells out with `E-<n>`). The two suite dirs were renamed lowercase; their
`task` fields stay `E-NNNN`. The guide now states the convention explicitly.

Two invariants deliberately preserved: relaxing case must not relax identity (a
manifest naming a different task than its directory still fails loudly), and
uppercase dirs still resolve, so the landed suites building
`.endless/tasks/E-1234/` fixtures (e-1611, e-1618, e-1791) are neither touched
nor broken.



### 5. verify.toml removed from the guide (commit 278b4715)

Also out of scope for reopen semantics; landed here at the user's direction
rather than as a separate task.

`docs/guide/orchestration.md` documented the per-task `verify.toml` manifest
with a full schema, a runner section, and (after item 4 above) a casing
convention. The manifest form is not the norm yet and will not be until the
verification-suite epic lands — several of its children are still open,
including the one that retrofits the existing `tests/tasks/*.sh` suites onto
the shared harness.

The guide is product documentation for every project that uses Endless, so
presenting an unshipped form as "the settled form" told every reader to author
something the product does not yet accept. That is not hypothetical: two
sessions, in two different conversations, specified a `verify.toml` deliverable
on the strength of it — this session did so in E-1916's plan and had to be
corrected.

Removed: the manifest schema section, the runner section (it only works against
a manifest), and the `verify.toml` mention in the topic cross-reference. Kept:
the `tests/tasks/e-<id>-verify.sh` convention that actually works today, plus a
one-line "Forthcoming" note that a declarative manifest and its runner are in
progress — no schema, nothing to author against prematurely.

The replacement text carries NO task ids. Endless's own ids are meaningless to
a reader working on another project, so "until <epic> lands" cannot be the
explanation the guide gives; "in progress" is. This applies to the guide
generally, and the guide currently violates it in roughly twenty other places
(`E-`/`ED-` references in orchestration.md, sessions.md, tasks.md,
reference.md) — not addressed here, and not filed, on the user's standing
instruction that task proliferation is a real cost.

Note that item 4's casing paragraph was removed by this commit, since it lived
in the deleted section. The code change from item 4 stands; only its guide
documentation is gone until the manifest form ships.

payload.title: Excise the web dashboard and its build stack from Endless
payload.description: Remove the web dashboard entirely. It is a proof-of-concept that will not be evolved: web work was deliberately halted to focus on the harder database, hooks, and workflow problems, and every task targeting it has been obsoleted. Keeping it costs a whole build toolchain (templ generation, tailwind CSS, templUI) and dependency surface that nothing else in Endless needs. Scope covers the internal/web package tree, internal/servecmd and its only caller, the Go and Python serve commands, the justfile recipes and their invocations from the aggregate build, the web-only Go module requirements, and the tracked generated artifacts. See analysis for the inspected scope. Out of scope: anything about a future web UI.
payload.analysis:
Remove the web dashboard entirely. It is a proof-of-concept that will not be
evolved: web work was deliberately halted to focus on the harder database,
hooks, and workflow problems, and every task targeting it has been obsoleted.
Keeping it costs a whole build toolchain and dependency surface that nothing
else in Endless needs.

Scope by inspection, to be re-verified at implementation time rather than
trusted from this description:

- The `internal/web` package tree (components, pages, templates, data, static,
  assets) and `internal/servecmd`, which is its only caller.
- The `serve` subcommand dispatch in the Go entrypoint, and the Python `serve`
  command that shells out to it including its port option and binary-watch
  restart loop.
- Justfile recipes and their invocations from the aggregate build: templ
  generation, the tailwind CSS build, the templUI symlink helper, and the dev
  watcher recipes that run them. The aggregate build recipe and the help text
  both name these and must stop doing so.
- Go module requirements that exist only for the web stack: the templ runtime
  and templUI. Check goldmark separately — the terminal renderer in
  `internal/mdterm` uses it independently and must keep working. Re-vendor
  after pruning.
- Tracked generated artifacts: the `*_templ.go` files and the built CSS output.
  Also the land-time handling that exists because these are build-regenerated
  and git-tracked.
- External tooling assumptions: templ and tailwindcss as prerequisites for
  building the project.

Verify afterward that a clean build, the full test suite, and vendoring all
succeed with the web toolchain absent, and that no remaining code imports the
removed packages. `internal/mdterm` carries a comment describing itself in
terms of the web markdown renderer; reword it so it does not reference a
package that no longer exists.

Deliberately out of scope: anything about a future web UI. When a web surface
is wanted again it will be preceded by research into whether Endless should
host it at all or whether a different tool should, with Endless integrating.
Do not file follow-on work for that here.

Fix session status all-clear hiding unpushed commits and failed git probes
payload.description: The unsettled/all-clear signal renders identically whether work is genuinely clear, whether a git probe failed, or whether the work is landed locally but unpushed. Observed live: 327 commits ahead of origin/main with session status showing a clean all-clear. Also makes the marker permanently absent on any project whose default branch is not 'main'. See analysis.
payload.analysis:
# Evidence

Observed live on 2026-08-10 while investigating a user report that
`session status` showed a task settled when the remote's main lacked its
latest commit.

## 1. Unpushed work is invisible

Unsettled is defined (ED-1540) as worktree vs LOCAL main: clean working tree
AND empty `main..HEAD`. Landing is a local rebase + fast-forward, so that IS
the right test for "did I land?" — but it stops there.

Measured at the time of the report:

    origin/main..main   327 commits   (unpushed)
    main..origin/main     2 commits   (unpulled — README edits made via GitHub)
    origin/main last fetched: 2026-08-09

The worktree tip was an ancestor of local `main` (settled — correct) and NOT
an ancestor of `origin/main`. So 327 commits existed only on one laptop while
`session status` rendered a clean all-clear.

The user read "settled", looked at the remote's main, did not find this
worktree's latest commit, and reasonably concluded the tool was lying. Both
facts were true simultaneously; nothing surfaced the second. The 2 unpulled
commits also mean local main cannot fast-forward push — likewise unsurfaced,
and one of the diverged files (README.md) is edited by the mermaid-sync
invariant, so a pull can conflict.

## 2. Every probe failure reads as settled

`UnsettledDetail.Unsettled()` (internal/monitor/worktree_unsettled.go) returns
false when:

- `WorktreePathForTask` → `ProjectPath(projectID)` fails (DB read),
- `git status --porcelain` errors (`StatusErr`),
- `git rev-list main..HEAD` errors (`RevListErr`).

The code documents this as deliberate: "Any git error is treated as settled:
the view must never block or lie because a git call hiccuped." For most views
that is right. For the one signal used to decide whether work is at risk it is
backwards — "I could not tell" is displayed as "you are clear".

## 3. Non-main projects are permanently blind

The rev-list probe hardcodes `main`; the source comment acknowledges it ("a
task branched off anything else is out of scope until that assumption is
lifted repo-wide"). Verified in a throwaway repo:

    $ git init -b master && ... && git rev-list main..HEAD --count
    fatal: ambiguous argument 'main..HEAD': unknown revision ...
    exit 128

That lands in case 2 and renders settled. Endless is a product for other
people's repositories, so every worktree in any project whose default branch
is not `main` shows a permanent false all-clear.

# Ruled out

- NOT a stale long-running monitor process. The user reproduced it with a
  fresh `endless session status`. (Separately noted: monitor panes DO hold a
  replaced binary image — one had been running 23 days against a
  `bin/endless-go` rebuilt by every `just land` — but that is not this bug.)
- NOT sandbox DB routing. All five running monitors had cwd = the main
  checkout, no `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, real DB.
- NOT a broken comparison. `main..HEAD` against LOCAL main is correct for
  "landed"; with a real unlanded commit, ◆ appeared correctly from both the
  worktree and the main checkout, and `task unsettled` named the commit.

# Root cause

The signal collapses three distinct states — "clear", "could not determine",
and "not examined" — into one glyph, and its horizon stops at local `main`.

# Open scope to settle when planned

- Is unpushed a distinct marker, or folded into ◆? They need opposite fixes
  (push vs land), which is the same argument ED-1540 made for splitting
  modified vs unlanded.
- Fetch, or compare only against the last-known `origin/*` ref? Fetching costs
  network and breaks offline; not fetching means the count is as stale as the
  last fetch, which must then be shown.
- How to resolve the default branch instead of hardcoding `main`.

triage.rationale: The description names three distinct failure symptoms but not how the status signal should distinguish clean/unpushed/probe-failed states or how to detect the default branch generically, leaving the design open.

# Decode BLOB-stored values at the DB read boundary

## Root cause

`endless task show <id> --text` crashes with `TypeError: write() argument must
be str, not bytes` when a task's text is stored with SQLite storage class BLOB
rather than TEXT. The chain: the row value arrives from sqlite3 as `bytes`,
`click.echo` takes its binary branch, and `_ColorProxy` — the stdout stand-in
that fixes `isatty()` so colorization follows an explicit decision — forwards
straight to a text stream in its `write`. The whole command dies with a raw
traceback naming no task and no field.

Exactly one value in the ledger is affected: `tasks.text` for E-449. Every
other value in every text-bearing column across tasks and decisions is TEXT or
NULL. Confirm this with a `typeof()` survey before starting rather than trusting
this statement.

The write path that produced it no longer exists. Every file read in the Python
package uses `read_text()`; there is no binary read. The row dates from an early
plan importer. Do not hunt for a live writer to fix — there isn't one.

## Prior art this extends

`get_conn` in the db module already solves the identical failure shape for a
different storage class. Read its comment first: E-1914 set a lenient
`text_factory` because sqlite3's default raises on invalid UTF-8 for the whole
QUERY, so one damaged byte took down commands that never asked for that column.
Its reasoning — apply at the connection rather than per query, because the
failure belongs to reading at all, and per-column fixes are whack-a-mole — is
the same reasoning that applies here, and the fix belongs beside it.

The gap E-1914 left is that `text_factory` governs only values SQLite hands
back as TEXT. A value stored as BLOB bypasses it entirely and arrives as
`bytes`. This task closes that gap.

## The fix

Extend the `row_factory` assignment in `get_conn` so bytes values are decoded
with the same lenient policy `text_factory` already uses:

    _conn.row_factory = lambda cur, row: sqlite3.Row(
        cur,
        tuple(
            v.decode("utf-8", "replace") if isinstance(v, bytes) else v
            for v in row
        ),
    )

This preserves the `sqlite3.Row` interface — key indexing and `keys()` both
continue to work — so no call site changes. Verified against a scratch DB
holding a BLOB in a TEXT-declared column.

Extend the existing E-1914 comment rather than adding a second block beside it;
the two halves are one policy about reading damaged values leniently, and
should read as one.

## Why decoding at this layer is safe

The schema declares no BLOB columns in any table. Any bytes value reaching a
caller is therefore an anomaly by definition, never intentional binary, so
there is nothing this can corrupt. Re-verify by searching the schema for BLOB
before landing; if that ever stops being true this fix needs revisiting.

## Do not fix in the renderer

`_ColorProxy.write` is where the crash surfaces, and hardening it there is the
tempting small change. Resist it: the proxy is installed only on some paths, so
the same bad value would still reach a real stdout on the others, and the next
consumer of a bytes-valued field breaks somewhere new. One decode at the read
boundary covers every command and every field at once.

## The fossil row

E-449's stored text can be repaired with a CAST to TEXT. This is optional — the
read fix renders it correctly either way, and the task is obsolete — but it
costs nothing and removes the only instance. Decide at implementation time; if
repaired, confirm the surveyed count of non-TEXT values drops to zero.

## Verification

- `endless task show 449 --text` renders the plan body instead of a traceback,
  both with and without `--paged`, and under `--no-color`.
- A regression test covering a BLOB-valued column read through `get_conn`,
  asserting a `str` comes back and the Row interface still works.
- The typeof survey across text-bearing columns reports no non-TEXT values.
- Full Python test suite passes.

payload.title: Fix just land aborting on unrelated enum drift when the worktree is behind main
payload.description: `just land` rebuilds the worktree's endless-go (E-1709) and then applies schema changes to the REAL DB with it — but only `endless worktree land`, which runs AFTER, rebases onto main. A branch that is behind main therefore rebuilds a still-stale binary, whose embedded enums lack rows main already applied to the real DB, and the enum-integrity check fails closed. Observed landing E-1898 from a worktree 147 commits behind: the abort named `gate_kinds row id=2 slug=relay`, which reads as database corruption but means 'your branch is stale'. E-1709's comment names this exact failure mode and solved only half of it — it makes the binary match the worktree's SOURCE, nothing makes the source match MAIN. Fix: make currency a precondition of the apply-change step, and make the integrity error name staleness when the DB has rows the binary lacks.
payload.analysis:
# Analysis

## What happened (observed, E-1898 land, 2026-08-10)

    → Rebuilding worktree endless-go before land (just go)
    → Applying schema change: internal/schema/changes/e-1898-processes-identity.go
    Error: apply-change failed: open db: gate_kinds integrity check on
      ~/.config/endless/endless.db: gatekind: gate_kinds row id=2 slug="relay"
      has no matching enum constant

Nothing was wrong with gate_kinds, and nothing was wrong with E-1898. The
worktree was 147 commits behind main. Main's E-1901 added `GateKindRelay = 2`
to the Go enum AND inserted the matching `gate_kinds` row, and that change was
applied to the real DB on 2026-08-06. The worktree's source predated it, so its
`gatekind` enum knew only `revisit`. The binary opened the real DB, ran
`gatekind.VerifyIntegrity`, saw a row it had no constant for, and failed closed.

Failing closed is CORRECT (E-1818): a binary must not operate on a database it
does not understand. The defect is that the land flow puts the binary in that
position, and then reports it as if the database were the problem.

## Root cause: the land guarantees the wrong currency

`just land` (justfile ~167-250) does, in order:

1. `just go` in the worktree — rebuild endless-go
2. `endless db apply-change <file>` against the REAL DB, using that binary
3. `endless worktree land` — which rebases onto main and fast-forwards

Step 1 was added by E-1709, whose own comment names this failure mode: "A
worktree rebased onto a newer main ... but not rebuilt would land with a STALE
binary whose embedded enums no longer match the real DB's rows ... (the E-1664
guard only checks the binary is PRESENT, not CURRENT)."

E-1709 solved half of it. It guarantees the binary matches the worktree's
SOURCE. Nothing guarantees the source matches MAIN. When the branch is behind,
`just go` faithfully rebuilds a still-stale binary and step 2 hits the same wall
E-1709 was written to prevent.

The rebase that would fix it is step 3 — after the step that needs it.

## Why it will recur and get worse

Any worktree that lives longer than main's next enum/schema change hits this.
The window widens the longer a branch runs, and long-lived branches are exactly
the ones with schema changes to apply. It is silent until land time.

## Directions (not locked)

- Make currency a precondition: before step 1, refuse (or rebase) when
  `git rev-list --count HEAD..main` != 0. Refusing is safer — an automatic
  rebase mid-land can stop on conflicts with main already partly advanced.
  Note E-1898's own rebase conflicted on the append-only db-ledger JSONL, so
  conflicts here are routine, not exceptional.
- Reorder so the rebase precedes apply-change, if that can be done without
  advancing main before the changes apply cleanly.
- Independently: make the enum-integrity error name the likely cause. Every
  VerifyIntegrity call site can say "this binary predates the database; rebase
  onto main and rebuild" when the DB has rows the binary lacks — that direction
  of drift is always staleness, never corruption. The reverse direction (binary
  has constants the DB lacks) is a genuinely missing migration and should keep
  reading the way it does now.

## Out of scope

E-1898 itself. Its branch was rebased onto main by hand and lands clean.

fields.title: Fix unsettled probe rendering failed git checks as settled
fields.description: UnsettledDetail.Unsettled() returns 'settled' — the all-clear — whenever its git probes could not run: project-path lookup failure, 'git status' error, or 'git rev-list' error. 'I could not tell' is rendered identically to 'you are clear'. The rev-list probe also hardcodes 'main', which exits 128 on any project whose default branch differs, so those projects show a permanent false all-clear and the marker can never appear. See analysis.
fields.analysis:
# What unsettled actually probes

Path is resolved by convention — `<project_root>/.endless/worktrees/e-<taskid>`,
`os.Stat`, must be a directory. Then exactly two git commands, both run with
`git -C <worktree>`. Nothing runs in the main checkout; nothing consults
`origin`.

    git -C <worktree> status --porcelain      # any output  -> modified
    git -C <worktree> rev-list main..HEAD --count   # > 0    -> unlanded

unsettled = modified OR unlanded (ED-1540).

# The defect

`UnsettledDetail.Unsettled()` (internal/monitor/worktree_unsettled.go) returns
false — settled, the all-clear — when the probes could not run at all:

- `WorktreePathForTask` -> `ProjectPath(projectID)` fails (DB read),
- `git status --porcelain` errors (`StatusErr`),
- `git rev-list main..HEAD` errors (`RevListErr`).

The code documents this as deliberate: "Any git error is treated as settled:
the view must never block or lie because a git call hiccuped." For most views
that is right. For the one signal a user relies on to answer "is any work at
risk?" it is backwards — "I could not tell" is rendered identically to "you
are clear."

## The trigger that makes it permanent: hardcoded `main`

The rev-list probe hardcodes `main`. The source comment acknowledges the
assumption ("a task branched off anything else is out of scope until that
assumption is lifted repo-wide"). Verified in a throwaway repo:

    $ git init -b master && git commit --allow-empty -m base
    $ git checkout -b feature && git commit --allow-empty -m work
    $ git rev-list main..HEAD --count
    fatal: ambiguous argument 'main..HEAD': unknown revision or path not in the working tree.
    $ echo $?
    128

That failure lands in the fail-open branch above and renders settled. Endless
is a product for other people's repositories, so on any project whose default
branch is not `main`, every worktree shows a permanent false all-clear — the
◆ marker can never appear.

# Root cause

The signal collapses "clear" and "could not determine" into one glyph.

# Explicitly OUT of scope

Local-vs-remote divergence (unpushed commits, `origin/main` ahead or behind).
`session status` answers "is this worktree's work landed into main?" — landing
is a local rebase + fast-forward, so LOCAL `main` is the correct reference and
the current comparison is right. Whether local main is pushed is a different
concern with a different owner and must not be folded in here. This is
recorded because it was conflated once during triage of this very report.

# Also ruled out (do not re-investigate)

- NOT a stale long-running monitor process: reproduced with a fresh
  `endless session status`. (Monitor panes DO hold a replaced binary image —
  one had run 23 days against a `bin/endless-go` that every `just land`
  rebuilds — but that is a separate issue, unfiled.)
- NOT sandbox DB routing: all five running monitors had cwd = the main
  checkout, no `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, real DB.
- NOT a broken comparison, and NOT triggered by the worktree merely differing
  from main. Direction is what matters. Observed case: worktree HEAD
  `debbb37a`, main HEAD `3a12b653`, different SHAs, but `main..HEAD` = 0 and
  `HEAD..main` = 4 (ledger commits written after the land). The worktree was
  BEHIND main, which is not work at risk. Settled was correct.
- With a genuine unlanded commit, ◆ appeared correctly from both the worktree
  and the main checkout, and `task unsettled` named the commit. The happy path
  works; only the error paths lie.

# E-1940 — Make the unsettled probe stop reporting "I could not tell" as "you are clear"

Absorbs E-1166. Decisions below are settled unless flagged OPEN.

## Problem

`UnsettledDetail.Unsettled()` returns false — the all-clear — whenever its git
probes could not run. The reaper runs the SAME two probes and already fails
closed ("Any git error while running 4 or 5 is treated as 'in use' — the reaper
would rather skip a candidate it can't reason about than destroy in-flight
work"). So the two surfaces the code claims agree on what "done and landed"
means actually diverge exactly where it matters, and the display picked the
unsafe polarity.

The hardcoded `main` is what makes this permanent rather than rare: on a repo
whose default branch differs, `git rev-list main..HEAD` exits 128 every time,
so `◆` can never appear and the reaper never reaps.

## Settled decisions

| # | Decision | Rejected alternative |
|---|----------|----------------------|
| 1 | Probe failure records a **fault** (E-698's system, already landed). | A new `?` glyph and legend entry. |
| 2 | Default branch resolved by one **shared helper**, used by the unsettled probe AND the reaper. | Fixing the display only and leaving the reaper on `main`. |
| 3 | E-1166 is **absorbed**: the Python `_default_base_branch` fix lands here too, under one strategy. | Two independent resolvers, one per language. |
| 4 | `Unsettled()` fails **closed** on probe failure. | Staying false; a third boolean. **(OPEN — confirm)** |

## A. Shared default-branch resolver

New `monitor.DefaultBranch(repoDir) (string, error)`. Resolution order:

1. `.endless/config.json` `default_branch`, when set — explicit beats detection.
2. `git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, stripped of `origin/`.
3. `git config init.defaultBranch`.
4. Probe `main`, then `master`, for an existing local ref.
5. Otherwise a real error — the caller decides, and no caller may silently
   substitute `main`.

Step 2 is unset on fresh clones (it needs `git remote set-head`) — that is
E-1166's original finding and why steps 3–5 exist. Resolution is per-repo and
should be memoized for the process; `session monitor` calls the probe every 2s
per row and must not add a git call per row per tick.

## B. Call sites

- `internal/monitor/worktree_unsettled.go` — `worktreeUnsettledAt`'s probe 2.
- `internal/monitor/reap_worktrees.go` — `maybeReapWorktree` condition 4.
- `src/endless/worktree_cmd.py` — `_default_base_branch` (absorbed E-1166).

The Go and Python implementations must agree on the order above; assert that in
the tests rather than trusting prose.

## C. Polarity and reporting

`UnsettledDetail` gains an explicit undetermined state rather than overloading
the existing booleans:

- `Unsettled()` returns **true** when a probe failed (fail closed).
- `IsUndetermined()` reports it distinctly, so `task unsettled` can say which
  probe failed and why. `Reason()` already prints the error text today — that
  half is honest and stays.
- The row renders the existing `◆`. No new glyph: the marker's job is "look
  here", which is correct for both real unsettled work and a failed probe.

A fault is recorded on probe failure, so the condition is visible even when no
one is looking at that row, and is clearable. Faults are deduped by
fingerprint — key on (task id, failing probe) so a monitor ticking every 2s
raises one incident, not thousands.

## D. Fault codes

Two new entries in `internal/faults/codes.go` (numbers never reused; take the
next free ids):

- **worktree-probe-failed** — `git status` or `rev-list` failed for a worktree.
  Severity `error`: the user asked "is my work safe?" and Endless could not
  answer.
- **default-branch-unresolved** — resolution fell through every step in A.
  Severity `error`, same reasoning; it disables the probe entirely.

Both carry the task id, worktree path, failing command, and git's stderr in
`Fields`/`Detail`.

## E. Reaper

Condition 4 takes the resolver. Its fail-closed handling is already correct and
must not be touched. Fixing the branch resolution is what lets a non-`main`
project reap at all — today every candidate errors and is skipped forever.

This change touches the code path that DELETES worktrees, so the tests must pin
that a resolver error still yields "skip", never "reap".

## Verification

**Durable tests** (these outlive the task):

- Go: resolver returns each step's answer in order, and errors rather than
  defaulting to `main` when all fail; `Unsettled()` is true on `StatusErr` and
  on `RevListErr`; `IsUndetermined()` separates that from real unsettled work;
  a fault is recorded once per (task, probe) rather than per tick; the reaper
  skips on resolver error.
- pytest: the Python resolver agrees with the Go order.
- A `master`-based fixture repo: `◆` appears for genuinely unlanded work and
  the reaper can reap. This is the regression that proves the product works
  outside `main`.

**`tests/tasks/e-1940-verify.sh`** — acceptance. **Author a script, NOT a
`.endless/tasks/e-1940/verify.toml`**: the manifest form is not the norm until
the verification-suite epic lands.

## Absorbed

- **E-1166** — absorbed; mark obsolete with an outcome naming this task.

## Not in scope

Local-vs-remote divergence (unpushed commits, `origin/main` ahead/behind).
`session status` answers "is this worktree's work landed into main?" — landing
is a local rebase + fast-forward, so LOCAL `main` is the correct reference and
the current comparison is right.

fields.outcome: Absorbed into E-1940. E-1166 identified that _default_base_branch in src/endless/worktree_cmd.py falls back to literal 'main' when 'git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD' is unset (fresh clones), which is wrong for master/develop repos. E-1940 hit the same defect on the Go side — the unsettled probe and the worktree reaper both hardcode 'main' in 'git rev-list main..HEAD' — and its plan specifies ONE shared resolution order (.endless/config.json key, then origin/HEAD, then init.defaultBranch, then probe main/master, then a real error rather than a silent fallback) applied to all three call sites, Go and Python. E-1166's proposed fallbacks (init.defaultBranch, ls-remote --symref) are preserved as steps in that order. Splitting the two would have meant two resolvers that could disagree about the same repo.

— Description —
One root cause, one visibility gap. ROOT: `ReapDeadTmuxPanes` NULLs `process` for panes it cannot see, deciding that from an ambient $TMUX it never validates — so a caller under a foreign tmux server nulls every session row in the project, and TouchSession's COALESCE (correct, added by E-1426) is left with nothing to protect; rows then read alive with no pane, forever. Observed 2026-08-05: 27 orphaned panes, 59 of 61 status lines blank. VISIBILITY: the status line collapses every failure into one placeholder, so it ran for hours untraced, and a not-ended row with no process is incoherent and must fail loudly. Umbrella: absorbs E-1895, E-1468, E-1408 (stale) and E-1642 (idle-timeout must fill the gap that guarding the reaper opens).

— Text —
# E-1898 — liveness is observed, never inferred

## The one-sentence change

Delete the reaper. Give every pane binding an identity that is unique across
tmux server lifetimes, observe liveness into a temp table per unit of work, and
JOIN. No code path may conclude a session is dead by looking at tmux and then
writing that conclusion to the `sessions` table.

## Why the previous plan was replaced

The prior plan guarded the destructive write with an escalating series of gates
(server-uuid gate, peer-server enumeration, ordering guarantees, forced
override). Every gate was an inference about whether the pane set in front of
the process was the right one to judge by, because no row recorded which tmux
server it was bound to. Stacking gates narrows the window; it cannot close it,
and each gate added edge cases and un-mockable tmux tests.

Recording the binding's server identity removes the need for every one of those
gates. This plan is shorter than the one it replaces because the complexity was
compensation for a missing column, not essential difficulty.

## Invariants — these are the acceptance criteria

**I1 — No inferred destructive write.** No code path writes `state='ended'`, or
clears a pane binding, based on an observation of tmux. Only reported facts (a
`SessionEnd` hook) and explicit operator action close a session. There is no
sweep, no reaper, no mass UPDATE.

**I2 — Bounded blast radius.** A failed or incomplete observation may affect at
most the rows it actually observed. `unknown` is NEVER converted to `dead` by
any consumer. An unreachable server costs zero rows.

**I3 — Identity unique across server lifetimes.** A tmux pane id reused by a new
server can never match a binding made against the old one.

**I4 — Tests need no tmux server.** Liveness is a JOIN against a table; tests
seed that table directly. No private tmux servers, no socket enumeration, no
seam counters.

Verification drives each invariant explicitly. I1 and I2 are the ones this task
exists for; a change that satisfies I3 but not I1 has not fixed anything.

## Model

Multiplexer-agnostic. tmux is one populator; cmux and herdr add their own
without touching consumers.

```
process_kinds(id, slug)          -- tmux | pid | ...   (mirrors session_kinds)

processes(                       -- DURABLE identity. A fact, kept forever.
  id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  kind_id       INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES process_kinds(id),
  server_uuid   TEXT,            -- tmux @server_uuid; NULL for kind=pid
  address       TEXT NOT NULL,   -- tmux pane id '%414'; or the pid as text
  first_seen_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  last_seen_at  TEXT NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE(kind_id, server_uuid, address)
)

sessions.process_id -> processes.id     -- replaces sessions.process

TEMP live_processes(kind_id, server_uuid, address, command)
TEMP observed_servers(kind_id, server_uuid)   -- which servers we actually reached
```

`processes` is append-mostly: a row is created the first time a session binds to
an address on a server, and is never deleted by observation. A tmux restart
mints a new `@server_uuid`, therefore a new `processes` row, therefore I3 holds
structurally — not by a guard that could be wrong.

## Liveness — three-valued, derived at read

```sql
CASE
  WHEN o.server_uuid IS NULL  THEN 'unknown'  -- server not reached
  WHEN l.address IS NULL      THEN 'dead'     -- reached; address absent
  ELSE                             'live'
END
FROM sessions s
JOIN processes p             ON p.id = s.process_id
LEFT JOIN observed_servers o USING (kind_id, server_uuid)
LEFT JOIN live_processes  l  USING (kind_id, server_uuid, address)
```

Expose as a view (`session_liveness`) so no consumer re-derives it.

Liveness is now PURELY OBSERVATIONAL: "is this address present on a server we
actually reached?" There is no remaining inference in it. That is the property
that makes I1 and I2 checkable rather than argued.

`unknown` is the safe branch: render last-known, condemn nothing. Per I2, no
consumer may map it to `dead`. The site that needs care is the spawn/claim
ownership guard — under `unknown` it must assume STILL OWNED and refuse. A
wrong refusal is an annoyance; the inverse steals a live worktree.

### Why the shell test is NOT part of liveness

The previous plan's death test was "address absent OR the pane runs a known
shell", to catch a killed harness whose pane survives. It is dropped from
liveness, because it is an inference and it can be wrong about a LIVE session:

- Verified 2026-08-09: a live Claude pane reports its version string
  (`2.1.220`) as `pane_current_command`, even mid-Bash-tool-call. So it does
  not collide with the shell set during normal operation.
- But **Ctrl+Z** puts the shell back in the foreground. A suspended-but-alive
  Claude session's pane reports `zsh`. Under the shell test that session reads
  `dead`, which drops its status line to the placeholder and — the part that
  matters — lets the spawn/claim ownership guard treat its task as free and
  hand the worktree to another session.

Cost of dropping it: a harness killed with its pane still open (SIGKILL, no
SessionEnd) leaves a stale-`live` row until the pane closes. That is a wrong
read in the SAFE direction — a refusal, never a theft — and E-1807's actual
case had a dead pane, which address-absence still catches.

`live_processes.command` is still collected, but is used ONLY for the cosmetic
"pane is running Claude but has no session row" status-line hint. An inference
is acceptable for a hint that misleads nobody and owns nothing; it is not
acceptable for liveness. That line is the rule, and the code must not blur it.

## Snapshot population

Refresh at the start of each **unit of work** — a CLI/hook invocation, an HTTP
request, a monitor repaint — inside the transaction that reads it, so a single
statement never sees two different observations.

For tmux: list sockets in `dirname $(tmux display-message -p '#{socket_path}')`;
for each, read `@server_uuid` and, when present, one
`tmux -S <sock> list-panes -a -F '#{pane_id} #{pane_current_command} #{pane_pid}'`.
Each successfully-read server contributes a row to `observed_servers`.

Enumeration stays, but is no longer load-bearing for safety: a server we cannot
reach (`tmux -S` outside the socket dir, relocated `TMUX_TMPDIR`) yields
`unknown` for its rows, not a verdict. This is the entire difference from the
previous plan's peer-enumeration gate, which had to be complete to be safe.

## Binding: where server_uuid comes from

The hook runs inside the pane. It reads `@server_uuid`; if absent it generates
and stamps one, exactly as `tmux init` does. Every binding therefore carries a
real server identity, and the previous plan's "refuse when uninitialized" gate
is unnecessary — identity is always present rather than sometimes checked.

## Deleted

- `monitor.ReapDeadTmuxPanes` and `internal/monitor/reap.go`, including the
  `len(alive) == 0` mass-UPDATE that ended every tmux row in one statement.
- `runInit`'s `runReset(nil)` call — the documented trigger for the 37-row batch.
- `endless tmux reset` ENTIRELY — the Go verb (`internal/tmuxcmd/reset.go`,
  its `tmux.go` dispatch), the Python wrappers (`cli.py` `tmux_reset`,
  `tmux_cmd.py` `run_reset`), the remedy line in `task_cmd.py:3304` that tells
  users to run it, and the assertion on that line in
  `tests/test_check_task_ownership.py:91`. No read-only replacement is
  introduced: `endless session list` and `endless sql` already read the view,
  and the ownership guard can no longer refuse over a gone pane — the snapshot
  shows it gone — so the remedy it advertised has nothing left to remedy.
- `TouchSession`'s collision invalidation. A reused pane is a different
  `processes` row, so the pane-reuse case cannot arise; a genuine same-server
  collision leaves both rows and the reader orders by `last_activity`.
- From the previous plan: D1, D2, D5, D6, D9 and their tests. D3's insight is
  kept as a read-time classifier; D7 and D8 survive as below.

## Kept from the previous plan

- **D7** — `runInit` no longer reaps (now: there is nothing to reap).
- **D8** — `runStatusLine` records a fault instead of silently rendering the
  placeholder on error. One correction to that decision: because
  `faults.Bind` is wired to `monitor.DB` (main.go:144) and `faults.Record`
  swallows its own DB failure by contract, this covers the non-DB fail-closed
  exits, not all of them. Worth doing; do not claim full coverage.
- The **ledger-safety assertion** in the verify suite.

## Migration

1. Create `process_kinds`, `processes`, add `sessions.process_id`.
2. Backfill, in TWO steps.

   2a. One `processes` row per distinct non-null `sessions.process`, with
   `server_uuid = NULL` (the binding server is not knowable retroactively) and
   `kind` derived from the string shape (`%N` -> tmux, `pid:N` -> pid).

   2b. ADOPT what is observable: for every pane live on the running tmux
   server, repoint the non-ended session bound to that address onto that
   server (`monitor.AdoptPaneBindings`).

   **Step 2b was missing from the first cut, and its absence took the board
   down on 2026-08-10.** This plan claimed the NULL-server rows would
   "self-heal on the session's next hook" and that live sessions would
   "recover within seconds without any repair verb". That is true only for
   sessions that FIRE hooks. An idle window fires none, and idle is the normal
   state, so every pre-existing session became unresolvable at once and STAYED
   unresolvable — the pane lookup matches on (current server uuid, address),
   and a NULL-server row matches no server at all. Measured on the real ledger
   when it bit: 64 sessions bound, 1 healed (the one firing hooks), 63 dark.

   Adoption is an observation, not a repair heuristic: a pane in the live set
   exists on the named server NOW. Two guards keep it honest — it refuses any
   address claimed by more than one non-ended session (that ambiguity is
   exactly what E-1898 exists to stop resolving by guesswork), and it creates
   a NEW row rather than stamping a server onto the shared NULL-server record,
   which the backfill deduplicates by address and which therefore carries
   history from every server that ever issued that pane.

   Panes that are not live, and every binding when no tmux server is
   reachable, keep `server_uuid` NULL and read `unknown` — never `dead`. On
   the measured ledger that left exactly one row: a genuine leftover from a
   dead server, which is precisely the case where `unknown` is the true
   answer. No repair verb is needed, but the reason is adoption, not healing.
3. Convert the ~35 call sites comparing `process` to a raw pane id. The type
   changes, so a missed site is a COMPILE ERROR — the property that made this
   safe to do where string-encoding `<uuid>:<pane>` would not have been.
4. Drop `sessions.process`.

`channels` is explicitly OUT OF SCOPE and keeps its string key; see E-1936.
It becomes the last consumer of the old key, deliberately, pending that
brainstorm's decision on whether it should exist at all.

## Tests — `tests/tasks/e-1898-verify.sh`

**Layer A — liveness truth table (FAIL-FAST, pure SQL fixtures, no tmux).**
Seed `processes`, `sessions`, `live_processes`, `observed_servers` directly and
assert every cell: server unobserved -> `unknown`; observed + address present ->
`live`; observed + address absent -> `dead`. Same pane id under two different
`server_uuid`s resolves independently (I3). Assert a pane running a shell reads
`live` while its session row stands — pinning that the shell inference is NOT in
the liveness path and cannot be reintroduced without failing this test.

**Layer B — invariants as tests, not as prose.**
- **I1:** grep the tree for any write of `state='ended'` or a binding clear
  outside the SessionEnd path; assert zero. Then drive a full hook cycle against
  an EMPTY `live_processes` (the exact 2026-08-05 shape: observer sees nothing)
  and assert **zero rows changed**. This is the regression test for the incident.
- **I2:** with `observed_servers` empty, assert no row reads `dead` and the
  ownership guard refuses rather than freeing.
- **I4:** the whole of A and B runs with `tmux` absent from `$PATH`.

**Layer C — one E2E** against a private tmux server (`-f /dev/null`, throwaway
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`) proving the populator fills the snapshot from a real server.
Exactly one, because the logic under test is now SQL, not tmux plumbing.

**Layer D — project-wide regression:** `go test ./...`, `just test`, `just build`.

**Ledger-safety assertion (mandatory).** Count non-ended sessions holding a
binding in the REAL database before and after the suite; they must be equal.

## Out of scope

- `channels` and the `endless-channel` MCP server (E-1936).
- Idle-timeout / session-duration truthfulness. Positive observation covers
  "Claude died, pane lives" without inferring death from silence.
- Non-tmux (`pid:`) liveness. The model has a slot for it; no populator ships here.
- Repairing rows damaged on 2026-08-05. Repaired by hand; migration step 2
  heals the rest on the next hook.

# Analysis

One root cause with four faces: **code and database versions diverge across the
worktree / main / real-ledger boundary, and nothing guards the seam.** All four
were hit for real on 2026-08-10, in one sitting, landing E-1898.

## Face 1 — the land uses a binary built from stale source

`just land` (justfile ~167-250) does, in order:

1. `just go` in the worktree — rebuild endless-go
2. `endless db apply-change` against the REAL DB, using that binary
3. `endless worktree land` — which rebases onto main and fast-forwards

Step 1 came from E-1709, whose comment names this failure: "A worktree rebased
onto a newer main ... but not rebuilt would land with a STALE binary whose
embedded enums no longer match the real DB's rows ... (the E-1664 guard only
checks the binary is PRESENT, not CURRENT)."

E-1709 solved half. It makes the binary match the worktree's SOURCE. Nothing
makes the source match MAIN. With the branch 147 commits behind, `just go`
faithfully rebuilt a still-stale binary and step 2 hit the same wall:

    Error: apply-change failed: open db: gate_kinds integrity check on
      ~/.config/endless/endless.db: gatekind: gate_kinds row id="2" slug="relay"
      has no matching enum constant

Nothing was wrong with gate_kinds. Main's E-1901 had added `GateKindRelay` and
applied the row; the worktree's source predated it. The rebase that would fix
this is step 3 — after the step that needs it.

## Face 2 — apply-change succeeds, the merge fails, the DB is left ahead

After rebasing by hand, the land was re-run. This time step 2 SUCCEEDED and the
land then failed, so main never got the code. Result: the real DB was migrated
to a schema only the unlanded branch understands, while every installed binary
still expected the old one. Every session query referenced a dropped column, so
all 64 sessions went unresolvable and session tracking froze machine-wide (0
writes in the following 7 minutes).

The justfile comment asserts: "If any apply fails, the land aborts before main
advances (clean recovery)." It reasons only about apply FAILING. Apply
succeeding and the merge then failing is the unhandled — and worse — case,
because it is the one that is irreversible.

## Face 3 — no supported way back

`endless db backup` exists and the land calls it. There is no `endless db
restore`. Recovery was an unguided `cp`, and it went wrong twice:

- Copied over a live database with six open connections, leaving a hot
  `endless.db-journal`. A read-only connection cannot roll back a hot journal,
  so every reader returned `database is locked` and the status bar flickered.
- The backup is produced by `VACUUM INTO`, which writes a **rollback-journal**
  database. The live DB was WAL. Restoring silently changed journal mode, and
  every connection then fought over an exclusive lock to switch it back.

Recovery took: `pkill -f 'endless task show'` (four abandoned pagers holding
connections for up to 22 days), killing two `session-status --monitor`
processes, then `sqlite3 <db> 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA integrity_check;'`
to roll back the journal and restore WAL. None of that is discoverable.

A backup you cannot safely restore is not insurance.

## Face 4 — the worktree hook runs candidate code against the real ledger

E-998 points a self-dev worktree's Claude hook at `<worktree>/bin/endless-go`,
and hooks force the REAL DB (E-1450). That is correct for ordinary branches and
BROKEN for any branch carrying an unlanded schema change: the candidate binary
writes a schema the real ledger does not have yet.

    endless-go hook: claude: touching session: upsert session:
      SQL logic error: table sessions has no column named process_id

Fired on every tool use for the duration. Non-blocking, so it degrades quietly:
the session simply stops being recorded. Worked around by hand-editing the
worktree's `.claude/settings.json` to point at `/usr/local/bin/endless-go`.

## Directions (not locked)

- **Currency precondition.** Before step 1, refuse when
  `git rev-list --count HEAD..main` != 0. Refusing beats auto-rebasing: E-1898's
  own rebase stopped on a conflict in the append-only db-ledger JSONL, and a
  rebase that stalls with main partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.
- **Ordering / atomicity.** Apply schema changes only once the merge is
  guaranteed, or make the pair recoverable as a unit. Face 2 is the expensive
  one; fix it even if nothing else here is done.
- **`endless db restore <backup>`.** A verb that stops DB users, restores, and
  re-establishes WAL — encoding what had to be reverse-engineered under
  pressure. Pairs with the backup the land already takes.
- **Schema-aware hook override.** When the worktree's branch adds an unapplied
  change file, `just claude-settings-init` should point the hook at the global
  binary rather than the candidate, and say so.
- **Diagnosis.** Every `VerifyIntegrity` call site can name the likely cause
  when the DB has rows the binary lacks: "this binary predates the database;
  rebase onto main and rebuild." That direction of drift is always staleness,
  never corruption. The reverse (binary has constants the DB lacks) is a
  genuinely missing migration and should keep reading as it does now.

## Out of scope

E-1898 itself, which is fixed and re-verified. `endless task show -p` pinning a
DB connection for the life of its pager is a real but separate nuisance; file it
on its own if it bites again.

# Analysis

## Why this is needed

`just land` takes a backup before applying a schema change, so the safety net is
already half-built. The other half does not exist: there is no way to use it.

On 2026-08-10 a land applied E-1898's migration to the real ledger and then
failed before merging, leaving the database on a schema no installed binary
understood. Session tracking froze machine-wide. Recovery was an ad-hoc `cp`,
and it went wrong twice before it went right:

1. **Copied over a live database.** Six connections were open (two
   `session-status --monitor`, four `endless task show -p` abandoned in pagers
   for up to 22 days). That left a hot `endless.db-journal`. A read-only
   connection cannot roll back a hot journal, so every reader returned
   `database is locked` and the tmux status bar flickered on and off.

2. **Journal mode silently changed.** `endless db backup` uses `VACUUM INTO`,
   which writes a **rollback-journal** database. The live DB was WAL. After the
   restore every connection fought for an exclusive lock trying to switch back.

What finally worked, none of it discoverable:

    pkill -f 'endless task show'          # abandoned pagers holding connections
    kill <session-status --monitor pids>
    sqlite3 <db> 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA integrity_check;'

## What the verb should do

`endless db restore [<backup>]` — default to the most recent backup.

1. Refuse unless the target is a real Endless DB and the backup opens clean.
2. Enumerate open connections (the equivalent of `lsof` on the db file) and
   REPORT them by pid and command. Do not kill anything silently; either refuse
   with the list, or require an explicit flag to proceed.
3. Restore the file.
4. Re-establish `journal_mode=WAL` and run `PRAGMA integrity_check`, failing
   loudly if it is not `ok`.
5. Keep the pre-restore database aside (timestamped) so the restore itself is
   reversible.

## Notes

- Step 2 is the load-bearing one. Every failure above came from copying over a
  file other processes had open, not from the copy itself.
- A dry-run mode that prints what it would do (holders, journal mode, sizes)
  costs little and is what you actually want at 5am mid-incident.
- Related: E-1941 covers the land-flow ordering that creates the need for a
  restore in the first place. This task is the recovery tool; that one is the
  prevention. They are independent — the tool is worth having regardless.

# E-1940 — Make the unsettled probe stop reporting "I could not tell" as "you are clear"

Absorbs E-1166. Decisions below are settled unless flagged OPEN.

## Problem

`UnsettledDetail.Unsettled()` returns false — the all-clear — whenever its git
probes could not run. The reaper runs the SAME two probes and already fails
closed ("Any git error while running 4 or 5 is treated as 'in use' — the reaper
would rather skip a candidate it can't reason about than destroy in-flight
work"). So the two surfaces the code claims agree on what "done and landed"
means actually diverge exactly where it matters, and the display picked the
unsafe polarity.

The hardcoded `main` is what makes this permanent rather than rare: on a repo
whose default branch differs, `git rev-list main..HEAD` exits 128 every time,
so `◆` can never appear and the reaper never reaps.

## Settled decisions

| # | Decision | Rejected alternative |
|---|----------|----------------------|
| 1 | Probe failure records a **fault** (E-698's system, already landed). | A new `?` glyph and legend entry. |
| 2 | Default branch resolved by one **shared helper**, used by the unsettled probe AND the reaper. | Fixing the display only and leaving the reaper on `main`. |
| 3 | E-1166 is **absorbed**: the Python `_default_base_branch` fix lands here too, under one strategy. | Two independent resolvers, one per language. |
| 4 | A probe failure marks the task's own row `◆`, alongside the fault. | Badge-only: `◆` keeps its narrow meaning and the row renders as if clean. |

## A. Shared default-branch resolver

New `monitor.DefaultBranch(repoDir) (string, error)`. Resolution order:

1. `.endless/config.json` `default_branch`, when set — explicit beats detection.
2. `git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, stripped of `origin/`.
3. `git config init.defaultBranch`.
4. Probe `main`, then `master`, for an existing local ref.
5. Otherwise a real error — the caller decides, and no caller may silently
   substitute `main`.

Step 2 is unset on fresh clones (it needs `git remote set-head`) — that is
E-1166's original finding and why steps 3–5 exist. Resolution is per-repo and
should be memoized for the process; `session monitor` calls the probe every 2s
per row and must not add a git call per row per tick.

## B. Call sites

- `internal/monitor/worktree_unsettled.go` — `worktreeUnsettledAt`'s probe 2.
- `internal/monitor/reap_worktrees.go` — `maybeReapWorktree` condition 4.
- `src/endless/worktree_cmd.py` — `_default_base_branch` (absorbed E-1166).

The Go and Python implementations must agree on the order above; assert that in
the tests rather than trusting prose.

## C. Polarity and reporting

`UnsettledDetail` gains an explicit undetermined state rather than overloading
the existing booleans:

- `Unsettled()` returns **true** when a probe failed, so the task's own row is
  marked. The alternative — report only in the badge and leave the row looking
  clean — was rejected: the row is the surface actually scanned, and a row that
  renders identically to a verified-clean one is the exact failure this task
  exists to remove. Marking the row is what tells you WHICH task is
  unverifiable without opening the fault.
- This widens `◆` from "you have work to land" to "look at this task — unlanded
  or uncheckable". That is a deliberate trade, and it is why the distinction
  below must be retrievable.
- `IsUndetermined()` reports it distinctly, so `task unsettled <id>` says which
  probe failed and why. `Reason()` already prints the error text today — that
  half is honest and stays. The list view collapses; the detail view explains.
- No new glyph, and no legend change beyond the fault badge E-698 already
  renders.

A fault is recorded on probe failure, so the condition is visible even when no
one is looking at that row, and is clearable. Faults are deduped by
fingerprint — key on (task id, failing probe) so a monitor ticking every 2s
raises one incident, not thousands.

## D. Fault codes

Two new entries in `internal/faults/codes.go` (numbers never reused; take the
next free ids):

- **worktree-probe-failed** — `git status` or `rev-list` failed for a worktree.
  Severity `error`: the user asked "is my work safe?" and Endless could not
  answer.
- **default-branch-unresolved** — resolution fell through every step in A.
  Severity `error`, same reasoning; it disables the probe entirely.

Both carry the task id, worktree path, failing command, and git's stderr in
`Fields`/`Detail`.

## E. Reaper

Condition 4 takes the resolver. Its fail-closed handling is already correct and
must not be touched. Fixing the branch resolution is what lets a non-`main`
project reap at all — today every candidate errors and is skipped forever.

This change touches the code path that DELETES worktrees, so the tests must pin
that a resolver error still yields "skip", never "reap".

## Verification

**Durable tests** (these outlive the task):

- Go: resolver returns each step's answer in order, and errors rather than
  defaulting to `main` when all fail; `Unsettled()` is true on `StatusErr` and
  on `RevListErr`; `IsUndetermined()` separates that from real unsettled work;
  a fault is recorded once per (task, probe) rather than per tick; the reaper
  skips on resolver error.
- pytest: the Python resolver agrees with the Go order.
- A `master`-based fixture repo: `◆` appears for genuinely unlanded work and
  the reaper can reap. This is the regression that proves the product works
  outside `main`.

**`tests/tasks/e-1940-verify.sh`** — acceptance. **Author a script, NOT a
`.endless/tasks/e-1940/verify.toml`**: the manifest form is not the norm until
the verification-suite epic lands.

## Absorbed

- **E-1166** — absorbed; mark obsolete with an outcome naming this task.

## Not in scope

Local-vs-remote divergence (unpushed commits, `origin/main` ahead/behind).
`session status` answers "is this worktree's work landed into main?" — landing
is a local rebase + fast-forward, so LOCAL `main` is the correct reference and
the current comparison is right.

payload.title: Decide how landed task branches stop accumulating already-landed commits
payload.description: A task branch keeps its pre-rebase commits after landing, because land rebases onto main (rewriting SHAs) and nothing resets the branch. It accumulates commits whose patches are already upstream while main moves ahead, so every later land replays the pile and the append-only ledger jsonl segments conflict once per ledger commit — recovery-and-retry never converges. Decide the mechanism: reset-after-land, drop patch-equivalent commits before replaying, refuse early with a named diagnosis, a union merge driver for the ledger files, extending reap to diverged branches, or a salvage-and-abandon path. See analysis for candidates, evidence, and the three gaps that fall out of the choice.
payload.analysis:
A task branch that has landed keeps its pre-rebase commits, because land
rebases onto main (rewriting SHAs) and nothing resets the branch afterward. The
branch therefore accumulates commits whose patches are already upstream, while
main moves ahead independently. Every later land from that worktree replays the
whole pile, and the append-only ledger jsonl segments conflict because both
sides appended different lines to the same file — one conflict per ledger
commit, so recovery-and-retry never converges.

Observed on the e-801 worktree, forked ten days earlier: `git cherry main HEAD`
reported all but three of its branch commits as patch-equivalent to commits
already on main, and the land aborted on the first ledger conflict. Comparing
trees rather than commits showed only two files where the branch was genuinely
ahead. That is the diagnostic worth generalizing: commit counts mislead here,
tree comparison and `git cherry` tell the truth.

Decide the mechanism. Candidates, none pre-selected:

- Reset the branch to main after a successful land, so the next land starts
  clean. Cheapest, but destroys anything genuinely unlanded that was not part
  of the landed set.
- Teach land to drop commits already patch-equivalent upstream before
  replaying, rather than replaying and conflicting.
- Detect the condition and refuse early with a named diagnosis, instead of
  discovering it as a mid-rebase conflict.
- Give the ledger jsonl files a union merge driver so concurrent appends stop
  conflicting at all. Fixes the symptom without addressing duplicate history.
- Extend the reap sweep to catch diverged branches, not only stale landed
  worktrees.
- Add a salvage-and-abandon path: take the files a stale branch is genuinely
  ahead on, record the landing, drop the worktree and branch. Today this is
  hand-run git plus `worktree land --record-only`.

Three concrete gaps are evidence, not separate tasks — their right fix falls
out of whichever mechanism wins:

- `worktree land --dry-run` does not simulate the rebase, so it cannot predict
  the failure it exists to preview.
- `worktree drop` documents a refusal for unlanded worktrees that its
  implementation does not perform; it checks foreign state and uncommitted
  changes only. Revisit after E-1898 and E-1941 land.
- No command performs the salvage composite, and `drop` leaves the branch
  behind, so abandoning a stale worktree cleanly still takes raw git.

Relates to E-1941, which fixes a different failure arising from the same root
condition: `just land` applies schema changes with a binary rebuilt from
still-stale worktree source, because the rebase onto main happens afterward.
That task makes currency a precondition of one step; this one asks why branches
go stale and stay stale at all.

Out of scope: the immediate disposition of any particular stranded worktree.

payload.title: Decide who may define, migrate, and use the DB schema, and when
payload.description: The 2026-08-10 incident produced four distinct failures from one question. `monitor.DB()` applies schema.sql on EVERY connection, so any binary additively migrates whatever DB it opens; E-1818's schema-passive mode stops that for pinned surfaces but only protects the DB from the binary, never the binary from the DB — a candidate binary against a main-schema ledger (or vice versa) passes connect cleanly and then fails at runtime writing or reading columns that aren't there. That is what took session tracking down for 30 minutes. Two hypotheses to evaluate: a migration-only executable built from the landing branch that does DDL and never DML; and replacing apply-on-connect with an explicit `endless db upgrade`, with ordinary connects verifying the schema version and refusing rather than silently fixing it. Analysis carries the full state tables. Deliverable is a decision plus follow-on tasks, not an implementation.
